subject: Physics
description: Refractive index, Snell's law, total internal reflection, lenses, prism dispersion

questions.stem: REFRACTION of light is the bending of a light ray when it passes from one medium to another due to:

options.option_text: A change in the colour of the light beam itself
A change in the speed of light between the media
A change in the direction the light source is facing
Reflection of light back into the original medium

questions.explanation: Refraction occurs because light travels at DIFFERENT SPEEDS in different media. In vacuum c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s; in water ~ 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s; in glass ~ 2 × 10⁸ m/s; in diamond ~ 1.24 × 10⁸ m/s. The bending follows Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. When light enters a DENSER medium it bends TOWARD the normal; entering a less dense medium it bends AWAY from the normal. Distractor 1 — colour can disperse but isn't the cause. Distractor 3 — source direction is irrelevant. Distractor 4 — reflection is a separate phenomenon.
questions.subject: Physics

options.option_text: Light strikes a denser medium at any angle of incidence
Light tries to leave a denser medium at angle exceeding the critical angle
Light is reflected back from a thick mirror surface to viewer
Two beams of light combine to produce a single brighter beam

questions.explanation: TIR — light traveling FROM a denser TO a less dense medium (e.g., glass to air) at an angle greater than the CRITICAL ANGLE bounces entirely back. Critical angle θ_c is given by sin θ_c = 1/n (n = refractive index of denser medium). For glass (n ≈ 1.5), θ_c ≈ 42°. For water (n ≈ 1.33), θ_c ≈ 49°. For diamond (n ≈ 2.42), θ_c ≈ 24° (gives diamonds their brilliance — light bounces around inside before exiting). Applications: OPTICAL FIBRES (light travels via TIR through cladded glass strands — basis of telecom + endoscopes), prismatic binoculars / periscopes.

questions.stem: When white light passes through a glass PRISM, it splits into seven colours because:

options.option_text: The prism adds new colours not present in white light
Different colours of light bend by different amounts on entry
Prisms randomly select colours to allow through the medium
Heat from the prism alters the wavelength of the light

questions.explanation: DISPERSION — refractive index of glass varies slightly with wavelength (n is highest for VIOLET, lowest for RED). So violet bends most, red bends least → white splits into the visible spectrum (VIBGYOR — violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red). Newton (1666) demonstrated this and showed a SECOND prism could re-combine the colours into white — proving white light is a mixture, not pure. Distractor 1 — colours are PRESENT in white, just unseen until separated. Distractor 3 — prism doesn't 'select'. Distractor 4 — heat doesn't change wavelength meaningfully.

questions.stem: If the absolute refractive index of a medium is 1.5, the SPEED of light in that medium is approximately:
questions.explanation: Refractive index n = c / v → v = c / n = (3 × 10⁸) / 1.5 = 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Distractor 4.5 × 10⁸ multiplies (faster than light, impossible). Distractor 3 × 10⁸ is c itself (vacuum value). Distractor 1 × 10⁸ uses n = 3.

questions.stem: A CONVEX LENS forms an image of a distant object at its:

options.option_text: Centre of curvature, twice the focal-length distance
Focal point, on the side opposite to the source
Optical centre, just inside the body of the lens
Pole of the lens, exactly at the front surface

questions.explanation: Parallel rays from a distant object converge at the FOCAL POINT (F) of a convex lens. Image is real, inverted, highly diminished. The focal length f is the distance from the optical centre to F. Used in telescopes (objective lens converges starlight at F), camera lenses, the eye's lens (forms image on retina). Distractor 1 = centre of curvature is for spherical mirrors, not directly for lenses. Distractor 3 = optical centre is inside the lens. Distractor 4 = pole is for mirrors.

questions.stem: A pencil partly dipped in water appears BENT at the water surface because of:

options.option_text: Reflection of light from the water's flat surface
Refraction as light bends entering and leaving water
Diffraction of light around the pencil's edges
Polarisation of light at the air-water boundary

questions.explanation: Light from the submerged part of the pencil bends as it leaves water (n=1.33) into air (n=1.00) — bends AWAY from the normal. Our brain projects the light back along straight lines, so the underwater part appears displaced (and so the pencil seems 'bent'). Same reason: a coin in a glass of water seems shallower than it is; rivers look less deep. Distractor 1 — reflection is from the surface (image flipped) but not the bend. Distractor 3 — diffraction is wave-spreading, different effect. Distractor 4 — polarisation does occur (Brewster's angle) but does not cause the bending appearance.

questions.stem: OPTICAL FIBRES used in long-distance telecommunication transmit light by exploiting:

options.option_text: Reflection from a polished metal coating outside the fibre
Total internal reflection inside the fibre's glass core
Diffraction of light around the fibre's circular cross-section
Scattering of light by particles dissolved within the glass

questions.explanation: Optical fibre = glass CORE (high n) surrounded by glass CLADDING (lower n). Light injected into the core hits the core-cladding boundary at an angle GREATER than the critical angle → totally internally reflected → bounces along the fibre with very low loss (~0.2 dB/km in modern silica fibres). Backbone of internet, undersea cables (e.g., the SEA-ME-WE network), endoscopes, hi-fi audio (TOSLINK). Distractor 1 — fibres don't use metal coating. Distractor 3 — diffraction is a different phenomenon. Distractor 4 — scattering would attenuate the signal, the OPPOSITE of what we want.
